metadata.topic: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table

questions.question: Define an atom, an element, a compound and a mixture. State how a compound differs from a mixture.
questions.modelAnswer: Atom: the smallest part of an element that can exist. Element: one type of atom only. Compound: two or more different elements chemically bonded in fixed proportions. Mixture: two or more substances not chemically bonded. Compounds require chemical reactions to separate; mixtures can be separated by physical methods.
markingPoints: Atom: the smallest part of an element that can exist. Element: one type of atom only. Compound: two or more different elements chemically bonded in fixed proportions. Mixture: two or more substances not chemically bonded. Compounds require chemical reactions to separate
mixtures can be separated by physical methods.

questions.question: A particle model uses ○ for oxygen atoms and ● for carbon atoms. Box A contains ○○, ○○ and ○○. Box B contains ●○○, ●○○ and ●○○. Box C contains ●, ○○ and ●○○. Identify A, B and C as an element, compound or mixture and justify each answer.
questions.modelAnswer: A is an element because it contains one type of atom. B is a pure compound because every particle contains carbon and oxygen atoms chemically joined in the same ratio. C is a mixture because different particles are present and are not all chemically joined to one another.
markingPoints: A is an element because it contains one type of atom. B is a pure compound because every particle contains carbon and oxygen atoms chemically joined in the same ratio. C is a mixture because different particles are present and are not all chemically joined to one another.

questions.question: For each mixture, name a suitable separation method and explain the relevant property difference: (a) insoluble sand and water; (b) dissolved sodium chloride and water when the salt is required; (c) ink dyes; (d) ethanol and water; (e) crude oil fractions.
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Filtration: sand particles are insoluble and too large to pass through filter paper. (b) Crystallisation/evaporation: water evaporates and salt crystallises. (c) Paper chromatography: dyes have different solubilities in the solvent and attractions to the paper, so travel different distances. (d) Simple/fractional distillation: different boiling points; ethanol vaporises first and is condensed. (e) Fractional distillation: hydrocarbons vaporise and condense at different temperatures.
markingPoints: (a) Filtration: sand particles are insoluble and too large to pass through filter paper. (b) Crystallisation/evaporation: water evaporates and salt crystallises. (c) Paper chromatography: dyes have different solubilities in the solvent and attractions to the paper, so travel different distances. (d) Simple/fractional distillation: different boiling points
ethanol vaporises first and is condensed. (e) Fractional distillation: hydrocarbons vaporise and condense at different temperatures.

questions.question: A dye spot travels 4.8 cm while the solvent front travels 8.0 cm. Calculate its Rf value. A pure reference dye has Rf = 0.60 in the same solvent. Explain what can and cannot be concluded from the result.
questions.modelAnswer: Rf = distance travelled by substance ÷ distance travelled by solvent = 4.8 ÷ 8.0 = 0.60. The spot may be the reference dye because the Rf values match under the same conditions. An Rf match alone does not prove identity; another solvent or analytical test can strengthen the conclusion. One spot suggests purity only under those conditions.
markingPoints: Rf = distance travelled by substance ÷ distance travelled by solvent = 4.8 ÷ 8.0 = 0.60. The spot may be the reference dye because the Rf values match under the same conditions. An Rf match alone does not prove identity
another solvent or analytical test can strengthen the conclusion. One spot suggests purity only under those conditions.

questions.question: State the relative mass, relative charge and location of a proton, neutron and electron.
questions.modelAnswer: Proton: mass 1, charge +1, nucleus. Neutron: mass 1, charge 0, nucleus. Electron: very small mass (about 1/1836), charge −1, shells/energy levels around the nucleus.
markingPoints: Proton: mass 1, charge +1, nucleus. Neutron: mass 1, charge 0, nucleus. Electron: very small mass (about 1/1836), charge −1, shells/energy levels around the nucleus.

questions.question: An ion of chlorine has atomic number 17, mass number 37 and charge 1−. Determine its numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons. Explain each value.
questions.modelAnswer: 17 protons because atomic number = proton number. 20 neutrons because 37 − 17 = 20. 18 electrons because a neutral chlorine atom has 17 electrons and gaining one electron gives a 1− charge.
markingPoints: 17 protons because atomic number = proton number. 20 neutrons because 37 − 17 = 20. 18 electrons because a neutral chlorine atom has 17 electrons and gaining one electron gives a 1− charge.

questions.question: Element X has two isotopes: X-63 has 69.2% abundance and X-65 has 30.8% abundance. Calculate the relative atomic mass to 1 decimal place and explain why isotopes have the same chemical properties.
questions.modelAnswer: Ar = [(63 × 69.2) + (65 × 30.8)] ÷ 100 = 63.616 = 63.6. Isotopes have the same number and arrangement of electrons, so react in the same way; they differ only in neutron number.
markingPoints: Ar = [(63 × 69.2) + (65 × 30.8)] ÷ 100 = 63.616 = 63.6. Isotopes have the same number and arrangement of electrons, so react in the same way
they differ only in neutron number.

questions.question: An atom has radius 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and its nucleus has radius 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Calculate how many times larger the atomic radius is. If the nucleus were represented by a 1 cm ball, calculate the model atom’s radius.
questions.modelAnswer: Ratio = 10⁻¹⁰ ÷ 10⁻¹⁴ = 10⁴ = 10 000. Model radius = 1 cm × 10 000 = 10 000 cm = 100 m.
markingPoints: Ratio = 10⁻¹⁰ ÷ 10⁻¹⁴ = 10⁴ = 10 000. Model radius = 1 cm × 10 000 = 10 000 cm = 100 m.

questions.question: Write the electronic structures of sodium (11), chlorine (17), calcium (20) and oxygen (8). For each, state its group and predict the ion it forms.
questions.modelAnswer: Na 2,8,1; Group 1; Na⁺ by losing one electron. Cl 2,8,7; Group 7; Cl⁻ by gaining one. Ca 2,8,8,2; Group 2; Ca²⁺ by losing two. O 2,6; Group 6; O²⁻ by gaining two. Main-group number is linked to outer-shell electrons.
markingPoints: Group 1
Na⁺ by losing one electron. Cl 2,8,7
Group 7
Cl⁻ by gaining one. Ca 2,8,8,2
Group 2
Ca²⁺ by losing two. O 2,6
Group 6
O²⁻ by gaining two. Main-group number is linked to outer-shell electrons.

questions.question: Describe how the atomic model changed from Dalton’s model to the modern nuclear model. Include Thomson, Rutherford’s alpha-scattering evidence, Bohr and Chadwick.
questions.modelAnswer: Dalton: solid indivisible spheres. Thomson discovered electrons and proposed the plum-pudding model: negative electrons in diffuse positive charge. Rutherford: most alpha particles passed through, so atoms are mostly empty space; some deflected, so positive charge/mass is concentrated in a tiny nucleus; very few rebounded, so the nucleus is small and dense. Bohr proposed electrons in fixed energy levels. Chadwick discovered neutrons in the nucleus.
markingPoints: Dalton: solid indivisible spheres. Thomson discovered electrons and proposed the plum-pudding model: negative electrons in diffuse positive charge. Rutherford: most alpha particles passed through, so atoms are mostly empty space
some deflected, so positive charge/mass is concentrated in a tiny nucleus
very few rebounded, so the nucleus is small and dense. Bohr proposed electrons in fixed energy levels. Chadwick discovered neutrons in the nucleus.

questions.question: In an alpha-scattering experiment, most alpha particles pass straight through gold foil, some are deflected and about 1 in 10 000 rebounds. Explain the three conclusions drawn from these observations.
questions.modelAnswer: Most pass through → atom is mostly empty space. Some deflect → positive charge is concentrated in a nucleus and repels positive alpha particles. Very few rebound → nucleus is extremely small, dense and contains most of the atom’s mass.
markingPoints: Most pass through → atom is mostly empty space. Some deflect → positive charge is concentrated in a nucleus and repels positive alpha particles. Very few rebound → nucleus is extremely small, dense and contains most of the atom’s mass.

questions.question: Explain how Mendeleev organised his periodic table and why scientists later accepted it.
questions.modelAnswer: He ordered mainly by relative atomic mass but changed the order where chemical properties required it; placed elements with similar properties in columns; left gaps for undiscovered elements; predicted properties of missing elements. Later discoveries closely matched his predictions, providing evidence for the table.
markingPoints: He ordered mainly by relative atomic mass but changed the order where chemical properties required it
placed elements with similar properties in columns
left gaps for undiscovered elements
predicted properties of missing elements. Later discoveries closely matched his predictions, providing evidence for the table.

questions.question: Explain how the modern periodic table is organised and how an element’s position relates to its electronic structure.
questions.modelAnswer: Elements are ordered by increasing atomic number. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer-shell electrons and therefore similar chemical properties. Period number gives the number of occupied electron shells.
markingPoints: Elements are ordered by increasing atomic number. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer-shell electrons and therefore similar chemical properties. Period number gives the number of occupied electron shells.

questions.question: Compare the typical ion formation and physical properties of metals and non-metals, and explain their positions in the periodic table.
questions.modelAnswer: Metals, mainly left/centre, lose electrons to form positive ions; usually conduct electricity/heat, are strong and malleable. Non-metals, mainly right, gain electrons or share electrons; generally poor conductors and, when solid, brittle. Position reflects outer-electron number.
markingPoints: Metals, mainly left/centre, lose electrons to form positive ions
usually conduct electricity/heat, are strong and malleable. Non-metals, mainly right, gain electrons or share electrons
generally poor conductors and, when solid, brittle. Position reflects outer-electron number.

questions.question: Describe and explain the trend in boiling point and reactivity down Group 0.
questions.modelAnswer: Noble gases are very unreactive because they have full outer electron shells. Boiling points increase down the group because atoms are larger/have more electrons, so intermolecular attractions between atoms are stronger and more energy is required to overcome them.
markingPoints: Noble gases are very unreactive because they have full outer electron shells. Boiling points increase down the group because atoms are larger/have more electrons, so intermolecular attractions between atoms are stronger and more energy is required to overcome them.

questions.question: Describe the reactions of lithium, sodium and potassium with water. Give the general products, balance the equation for sodium, and state the observations and pH of the solution.
questions.modelAnswer: Metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen. 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Metals float/move, fizz as hydrogen forms and disappear; sodium may melt, potassium may ignite with a lilac flame. The solution is alkaline, pH greater than 7, because hydroxide ions form.
markingPoints: Metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen. 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Metals float/move, fizz as hydrogen forms and disappear
sodium may melt, potassium may ignite with a lilac flame. The solution is alkaline, pH greater than 7, because hydroxide ions form.

questions.question: Explain why Group 1 metals become more reactive down the group.
questions.modelAnswer: Each atom has one outer electron. Down the group there are more shells, greater distance and more shielding. Attraction between the nucleus and outer electron is weaker, so the electron is lost more easily and reactivity increases.
markingPoints: Each atom has one outer electron. Down the group there are more shells, greater distance and more shielding. Attraction between the nucleus and outer electron is weaker, so the electron is lost more easily and reactivity increases.

questions.question: Chlorine water is added separately to potassium bromide and potassium iodide solutions. Bromine water is added to potassium chloride solution. Predict the outcomes, give colour observations, and write ionic equations for reactions that occur.
questions.modelAnswer: Chlorine displaces bromide: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂; solution becomes orange. Chlorine displaces iodide: Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂; solution becomes brown. Bromine does not displace chloride because bromine is less reactive than chlorine.
markingPoints: Chlorine displaces bromide: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂
solution becomes orange. Chlorine displaces iodide: Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂
solution becomes brown. Bromine does not displace chloride because bromine is less reactive than chlorine.

questions.question: Explain why halogens become less reactive down Group 7 and predict the state and colour trend.
questions.modelAnswer: Halogens react by gaining one electron. Down the group, more shells increase distance and shielding, weakening nuclear attraction for an incoming electron, so reactivity decreases. Melting/boiling points increase; colours become darker and physical state changes gas → liquid → solid.
markingPoints: Halogens react by gaining one electron. Down the group, more shells increase distance and shielding, weakening nuclear attraction for an incoming electron, so reactivity decreases. Melting/boiling points increase
colours become darker and physical state changes gas → liquid → solid.

questions.question: Compare transition metals with Group 1 metals and state three characteristic properties of transition metals.
questions.modelAnswer: Transition metals are less reactive, harder/stronger, denser and have higher melting points than Group 1 metals. They often form coloured compounds, can form ions with different charges, and many act as catalysts.
markingPoints: Transition metals are less reactive, harder/stronger, denser and have higher melting points than Group 1 metals. They often form coloured compounds, can form ions with different charges, and many act as catalysts.

questions.question: Balance the equation for magnesium reacting with oxygen and explain what the equation shows about atoms. __Mg + __O₂ → __MgO
questions.modelAnswer: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. It shows the same number of each type of atom before and after the reaction; atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed.
markingPoints: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. It shows the same number of each type of atom before and after the reaction
atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed.

questions.question: A mixture contains sand and dissolved sodium chloride. Describe how to obtain dry samples of both substances.
questions.modelAnswer: Filter: sand remains as residue; wash with distilled water and dry. Heat the filtrate gently to evaporate some water, cool to crystallise sodium chloride, filter and dry the crystals.
markingPoints: Filter: sand remains as residue
wash with distilled water and dry. Heat the filtrate gently to evaporate some water, cool to crystallise sodium chloride, filter and dry the crystals.

questions.question: Explain why fractional distillation, rather than filtration, can separate a mixture of ethanol and water.
questions.modelAnswer: Both liquids pass through filter paper, so filtration cannot separate them. They have different boiling points; heat the mixture, the lower-boiling component vaporises more readily, then condense and collect it.
markingPoints: Both liquids pass through filter paper, so filtration cannot separate them. They have different boiling points
heat the mixture, the lower-boiling component vaporises more readily, then condense and collect it.

questions.question: An atom has electron arrangement 2,8,3. State its period and group, predict the ion formed and explain how it forms.
questions.modelAnswer: Period 3; Group 3 (AQA group convention); loses three outer electrons to obtain a full outer shell; forms a 3+ ion.
markingPoints: Period 3
Group 3 (AQA group convention)
loses three outer electrons to obtain a full outer shell
forms a 3+ ion.

questions.question: For ²⁴₁₂Mg and ²⁶₁₂Mg, state what is the same and different and calculate the neutron number of each isotope.
questions.modelAnswer: Both have 12 protons and, if neutral, 12 electrons; they are the same element. Neutrons: 24−12=12 and 26−12=14.
markingPoints: Both have 12 protons and, if neutral, 12 electrons
they are the same element. Neutrons: 24−12=12 and 26−12=14.

questions.question: The boiling points of lithium, sodium and potassium are 1342, 883 and 759 °C. Describe the trend and predict a reasonable boiling point for rubidium.
questions.modelAnswer: Boiling point decreases down the group. A prediction below 759 °C, with sensible extrapolation (about 650–700 °C), is supported; exact value not required.
markingPoints: Boiling point decreases down the group. A prediction below 759 °C, with sensible extrapolation (about 650–700 °C), is supported
exact value not required.

questions.question: Iodine solution is added to sodium bromide solution. State whether a reaction occurs and explain using Group 7 reactivity.
questions.modelAnswer: No reaction. Iodine is below bromine and is less reactive, so it cannot displace bromide ions from sodium bromide.
markingPoints: No reaction. Iodine is below bromine and is less reactive, so it cannot displace bromide ions from sodium bromide.

questions.question: Explain why argon is used in filament lamps and helium is used in balloons.
questions.modelAnswer: Argon is unreactive because it has a full outer shell, so it does not react with the hot filament. Helium is unreactive and less dense than air, so balloons rise and it does not burn.
markingPoints: Argon is unreactive because it has a full outer shell, so it does not react with the hot filament. Helium is unreactive and less dense than air, so balloons rise and it does not burn.

questions.question: Give two examples of transition metals or their compounds used as catalysts and state the process or reaction involved.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples: iron in the Haber process; nickel in hydrogenation of alkenes/vegetable oils; vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process; manganese dioxide for hydrogen peroxide decomposition. Any two correct linked examples.
markingPoints: Examples: iron in the Haber process
nickel in hydrogenation of alkenes/vegetable oils
vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process
manganese dioxide for hydrogen peroxide decomposition. Any two correct linked examples.

questions.question: Rutherford expected alpha particles to pass through the plum-pudding atom. Explain why the rare large deflections caused the model to be rejected.
questions.modelAnswer: Diffuse positive charge could not exert the concentrated repulsion needed for large deflections. Rare rebounds showed most mass and positive charge occupy a tiny dense nucleus, so the plum-pudding model was inconsistent with evidence.
markingPoints: Diffuse positive charge could not exert the concentrated repulsion needed for large deflections. Rare rebounds showed most mass and positive charge occupy a tiny dense nucleus, so the plum-pudding model was inconsistent with evidence.

questions.question: Element X has isotopes X-63 (69.2%) and X-65 (30.8%). Calculate its relative atomic mass.
Explain why successive ionisation energies provide evidence that electrons occupy shells.
questions.modelAnswer: A large jump occurs after all electrons in an outer shell are removed; the next electron is closer to the nucleus, less shielded and more strongly attracted, so much more energy is required.
markingPoints: A large jump occurs after all electrons in an outer shell are removed
the next electron is closer to the nucleus, less shielded and more strongly attracted, so much more energy is required.

questions.question: An ion has 17 protons, 18 electrons and 20 neutrons. State its symbol including mass number and charge, and explain each part.
questions.modelAnswer: Atomic number 17 identifies chlorine; mass number = 17 + 20 = 37; one extra electron gives charge −1, so ³⁷₁₇Cl⁻.
markingPoints: Atomic number 17 identifies chlorine
mass number = 17 + 20 = 37
one extra electron gives charge −1, so ³⁷₁₇Cl⁻.

questions.question: Explain how the alpha-scattering results led Rutherford to replace the plum-pudding model.
questions.modelAnswer: Most alpha particles passed through, showing atoms are mostly empty space. Some deflected, showing concentrated positive charge. Very few rebounded, showing a tiny, dense nucleus containing most mass.
markingPoints: Most alpha particles passed through, showing atoms are mostly empty space. Some deflected, showing concentrated positive charge. Very few rebounded, showing a tiny, dense nucleus containing most mass.

questions.question: Predict and explain the relative reactivity of potassium and lithium.
questions.modelAnswer: Potassium is more reactive. Its outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so nuclear attraction is weaker and the electron is lost more easily.
markingPoints: Potassium is more reactive. Its outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so nuclear attraction is weaker and the electron is lost more easily.

questions.question: Explain how the results of the alpha-scattering experiment led scientists to replace the plum-pudding model.
questions.modelAnswer: Most alpha particles passed through, showing atoms are mostly empty space. Some were deflected, showing positive charge and mass are concentrated. Very few rebounded, showing a tiny, dense nucleus. The evidence contradicted diffuse positive charge in the plum-pudding model.
markingPoints: Most alpha particles passed through, showing atoms are mostly empty space. Some were deflected, showing positive charge and mass are concentrated. Very few rebounded, showing a tiny, dense nucleus. The evidence contradicted diffuse positive charge in the plum-pudding model.

questions.question: Explain why a scientific model may be changed even when the earlier model was useful.
questions.modelAnswer: Models are simplified explanations based on available evidence. New observations that the model cannot explain require it to be modified or replaced; usefulness does not make a model permanently true.
markingPoints: Models are simplified explanations based on available evidence. New observations that the model cannot explain require it to be modified or replaced
usefulness does not make a model permanently true.

questions.question: A mass spectrum gives relative abundances of 75% for mass 35 and 25% for mass 37. Calculate the relative atomic mass.
Explain why repeating a measurement cannot correct a balance that always reads 0.20 g too high.
questions.modelAnswer: The offset is a systematic error, so every repeat is shifted in the same direction. Repeats reduce the effect of random error but not systematic error; zero or calibrate the balance.
markingPoints: The offset is a systematic error, so every repeat is shifted in the same direction. Repeats reduce the effect of random error but not systematic error
zero or calibrate the balance.

questions.question: A student reports the mass of a sample as 2.347891 g using a balance with 0.01 g resolution. Evaluate the reported value.
questions.modelAnswer: The balance cannot justify more than two decimal places. The result should be reported as 2.35 g; extra digits imply false precision.
markingPoints: The balance cannot justify more than two decimal places. The result should be reported as 2.35 g
extra digits imply false precision.

questions.question: Describe how evidence from several independent experiments increases confidence in an atomic model.
questions.modelAnswer: Different methods test different predictions and have different limitations. Consistent results are less likely to be due to one apparatus error, bias or chance, so confidence increases.
markingPoints: Different methods test different predictions and have different limitations. Consistent results are less likely to be due to one apparatus error, bias or chance, so confidence increases.
